newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Telecoms firms seen as investment source -execs.
newsitem.headline: Telecoms firms seen as investment source -execs.

text.p: Telecommunications companies are likely to be a prime source of Asia's infrastructure investment in the next century, industry executives said on Friday.
"We (the industry) are becoming more and more positioned as the underlying platform to support infrastructure building," said John Black, senior vice president for telecommunications at Oracle Corp.

"Telecommunications companies are a fundamental part of the economic infrastructure of growth in Asia," Chris Rooney, president of global sales at Global One, told Reuters at the Asia Telecoms 97 trade fair.
"We play a supportive and participative role to bring countries forward and help bring economies forward," Rooney said.
The investment being pumped into global telecommunications infrastructures is huge. Analysts estimate up to US$2 trillion could be poured in over the next decade.
World Bank figures suggest that at least US$60 billion a year will need to be spent in Asia over the next five years just to meet present levels of demand telecommunications services.
Two thirds of Asia's people, many of them living in remote rural areas, do not have a telephone.
The cost of extending services to these areas is seen to be prohibitive for governments, with only private sector firms having the resources and the will to invest.

Christopher Galvin, chief executive of Motorola Corp, said his company recognised it had a role to play as a responsible corporate citizen in the developing world and that the telecommunications networks it created helped enhance economic growth.
"We help build the overall society and create conditions for generating wealth that benefits the whole society," Galvin said.
Adi Adiwoso, president of Indonesia's Pasifik Satelit Nusantara, said "the whole telecommunications budget (of Indonesia) comes outside the scope of the government now".
Adiwoso said the role of governments was increasingly to tell private companies what countries needed in terms of infrastructure and let them get on with it.

The result would be that money saved by governments no longer spending vast sums on telecommunications infrastructure could be channelled into other public projects like road building, water supply and power plant construction.
"Governments will say we want to do this, this and this and then tell us (private operators) to do it," Adiwoso said.

But profit would not give way to philanthropy: "The only reason I'm in this business is because I'm making money, not because I'm philanthropic," Adiwoso said, adding that low cost telecommunications services could yield good profits.
"You can reduce the price of telecommunications because the volume gets bigger at little extra cost. In other words you still make money," he said.
